verdicts.rewritten_summary: BuzzFeed feature (Rozenn Le Carboulec) on trans women in French prisons: Article D248 of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates separate establishments for men and women, so placement follows the sex on identity documents and trans women are typically held in men's facilities - as of 1 Nov 2016 there were 13 transgender detainees held across eight establishments, most at Fleury-Mérogis. Profiles Paola, an Argentine trans woman transferred to a men's facility in 2014 and met with shouts of 'We don't want any women here', despite a passport listing her as female, because French law does not recognise her Argentine legal gender for placement purposes. Documents inconsistent access to treatment and a 2,000-euro symbolic damages award over detention conditions, with the justice minister pressed to amend D248.

Opinion of the Contrôleur général des lieux de privation de liberté (CGLPL), France's national preventive mechanism, dated 25 May 2021, on the care of transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: building on referrals received since 2010 and a 2010 opinion on transsexual prisoners, it covers all places of deprivation of liberty. Inspections cited include Saint-Martin-de-Ré and Toulouse-Seysses prisons and the Toulouse central police station, with evidence from eight transgender women; it documents discrimination, stigmatisation and health/social-care blind spots and recommends policies to combat the discrimination and exclusion they face, referencing law n° 2016-1547 of 18 November 2016 on justice modernisation/prison transfers and the 'racism, antisemitism, LGBT and discrimination' referents appointed since 2018. This is the basis for the record's claim that the CGLPL reports persistent serious violations of trans detainees' rights across inspected prisons.

Outright International (IGLHRC) Philippines country overview (updated 2025): same-sex relations are legal and acceptance indices rank the country among the most accepting in Asia, but trans people cannot access legal gender recognition - the 2001 Clerical Error Law (RA 9048) blocks gender-marker correction - and national non-discrimination bills filed since 1999 remain unenacted, with two civil-union bills filed since 2022 facing religious-conservative opposition; non-discrimination ordinances exist at barangay, city, municipal and provincial levels. A 2018 SWS survey found only 22% of Filipinos supported same-sex civil unions and a majority opposed trans women's access to women's toilets. The Safe Spaces Act criminalises homophobic and transphobic slurs; the Anti-Bullying Act and the Gender-Responsive Basic Education Policy (reiterated 2022, June designated Pride Month) cover sexual orientation and gender identity in schools; Executive Orders No. 100 (2019) and No. 51 (2023) creating the national Diversity and Inclusion Program remain unimplemented as of 2025.

Bulatlat (26 Jun 2025): 18-year-old trans woman Kierra Apostol, a Cagayan State University business-management student, was found dead in a Cagayan province river on 23 June 2025 days after being reported missing, with signs of physical assault; a criminology student who admitted driving her surrendered to police while denying involvement. A second killing that same day - trans woman and former activist-journalist Ali Macalintal shot by an unidentified gunman inside an acupuncture clinic in General Santos - is reported alongside, and Bahaghari and other groups cite the cases in calling for passage of the SOGIESC Equality Bill, stuck in Congress for 25 years (latest version Senate Bill 1600), which would prohibit admission denial, denial of public and health services, and infliction of physical harm or verbal abuse based on SOGIE.
